newsitem.title: PERU: Peru promises safety of hostages is priority.
newsitem.headline: Peru promises safety of hostages is priority.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori promised on Thursday in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of hostages will be his first priority in resolving the guerrilla siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

"I want to assure your excellency that I am occupying myself permanently and jointly with my team to achieve a solution as soon as possible to this crisis, the principal objective being the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," Fujimori wrote in the letter.

Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, has held three emergency cabinet meetings but still has not made a public statement to the Peruvian people since the crisis began on Tuesday night.
On Thursday evening he held a one-hour emergency meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived earlier in the day to help negotiate the crisis.
The heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas released four more captives earlier on Thursday as talks continued over the fate of about 400 remaining hostages.

The rebels have threatened to kill their captives, who include many high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials, if the Peruvian government does not release up to 500 of their imprisoned comrades.
Clinton had said Washington was "very concerned" about the captives, and Fujimori, in his letter, promised to telephone him as soon as possible.
Meanwhile Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram said in Quito on Thursday he was ready to grant asylum to the rebels.

"We have stated clearly that if we can be of help, providing the Peruvian government asks for it, we would accede to that," Bucaram said when asked by journalists whether Ecuador would give asylum to the guerrillas.
Witnesses outside the ambassador's residence reported earlier that two shots were heard at about 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT) from inside the compound, which was seized on Tuesday.
But Red Cross officials, who were entering the building to mediate and supply food and medical equipment, said the shots caused no injuries.
The four released hostages, all dressed in suits and looking dazed, were two Japanese businessmen and two Peruvians including a local representative of Nissan.
Negotiations, headed by the Red Cross, brought no early breakthrough in the crisis.

Michel Minning, a Swiss national of the Red Cross leading talks with the rebels, was also conducting the supply operation, which even included delivering three chess sets and 200 rosary chains to the residence along with food and water.

Four ambassadors, released on Wednesday, were also "acting as a link for commmunications between the Japanese residence and authorities outside," Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent told a news conference. The other "hostages on parole" were the ambassadors of Germany, Heribert Woeckel, and Greece, Alcibiadis Karokis as well as a Peruvian ambassador, Armando Lecaros, Vincent said.
The ambassador, who spent about 30 minutes in the compound early on Thursday, said: "Discussions were cordial, the hostages were in good condition.
"People are behaving magnificently ... Both the hostages and the members of the MRTA have behaved with restraint."
The hostages -- all men since the release late on Tuesday of women captives -- were sleeping on the floor in cramped conditions and living on a sparse diet.
A letter faxed early on Wednesday from the residence to family members of hostages and signed by captives said there were 490 hostages. Six have been released since then.
The Red Cross put the number at 380.

Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages. The embassy residence is legally Japanese territory, meaning in theory Fujimori would need Tokyo's approval for an assault.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy attended the reception, but left before the siege.

The rebels, who include three non-Peruvians, assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the building beforehand among flowers and inside a Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, reportedly had planned to attend the party but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
